# Results — Study 480 (Darvas Box)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **the box
breakout forecasts continuation: a close above the box top is a high-probability long** — encoded
as a mechanical rule. The box top is the highest close over a trailing 20-day window (used only
after the close has sat below it for ≥ 5 consecutive bars, so a consolidation has formed); a long
fires on the first close above the box top, entered at the **next close** (one documented lag),
with an ATR/box stop, and we measure the forward 5/10/20/60-day return. Offline & deterministic
once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Entries | **949** mechanical box breakouts pooled across the 5 tapes (lookback = 20, min-box = 5) |
| Timing / costs | box top/bottom from **trailing** bars only; enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per breakout |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid ETFs; this is a
> single-instrument momentum study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so survivorship affects only the
> drift baseline (which is exactly what the random-entry control neutralizes).

## The signal — box breakout vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**Welch breakout-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = breakout − random.

| horizon | n | breakout | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (breakout−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 946 | +25.8 bps | 61% | +3.48 | +42.3 bps | **−16.4 bps** | +23.8 bps | −1.56 | 0.119 |
| 10-day | 945 | +48.4 bps | 63% | +5.22 | +63.2 bps | **−14.8 bps** | +46.4 bps | −1.00 | 0.318 |
| 20-day | 943 | +94.1 bps | 65% | +6.41 | +102.3 bps | **−8.2 bps** | +92.1 bps | −0.38 | 0.702 |
| 60-day | 938 | +248.8 bps | 68% | +6.67 | +258.0 bps | **−9.2 bps** | +246.8 bps | −0.26 | 0.798 |

Read it carefully. The one-sample *t* against zero looks spectacular (**+6.41** at 20 days,
**+6.67** at 60) — but that is **pure beta**: long-only entries on an upward-drifting index inherit
the drift. Against the **drift-matched random baseline**, the box breakout is *worse* at **every**
horizon (Δ = −16.4 / −14.8 / −8.2 / −9.2 bps) and the breakout-minus-random difference **never
clears the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar** (the most negative Welch *t* is −1.56 at 5 days, *p* = 0.119; it is
never positive). The breakout does not forecast — it slightly underperforms a coin-flip entry.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — the breakout loses to random in 3 of 5 names

| ticker | entries | breakout | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (breakout−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 201 | +119.8 bps | +5.25 | +116.0 bps | **+3.8 bps** |
| QQQ | 197 | +137.1 bps | +4.11 | +123.2 bps | **+13.9 bps** |
| IWM | 186 | +69.7 bps | +1.76 | +113.7 bps | **−44.0 bps** |
| DIA | 194 | +73.1 bps | +2.89 | +75.1 bps | **−2.0 bps** |
| GLD | 171 | +64.8 bps | +1.59 | +81.0 bps | **−16.2 bps** |

The tiny positive deltas in SPY/QQQ (+3.8 / +13.9 bps) are inside the noise; IWM is **−44 bps**
behind a dart. No coherent cross-sectional edge — the hallmark of relabelled drift.

## Geometry placebo — destroy the box timing, nothing changes

The decisive "does the box geometry matter?" test: keep the marginal (same instrument, epoch,
hold) and the same trade *count*, but scatter the entry dates at random, so the specific
box-top-breakout timing is destroyed. If the breakout genuinely forecast, the observed return
would sit far in the right tail of the scattered distribution.

| test | observed breakout 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY shuffled-box | +119.8 bps | **0.192** | 500 |

**19% of randomly-scattered entries match or beat the real breakout** (*p* = 0.192). The box-top
timing carries no extra information — random dates do as well. "The box breakout forecasts" is
busted.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real continuation

On a deterministic tape with a *planted* post-breakout continuation (knob `edge`), the same
breakout rule behaves exactly as it must — so the flat real-tape result is a genuine "nothing
there", not a dead detector.

| planted edge | n | breakout | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no continuation) | 127 | −59.1 bps | 46% | −1.56 |
| **0.30** (real planted continuation) | 119 | +458.6 bps | 78% | **+9.77** |

With no planted continuation the control sits at *t* = −1.56 (does not clear 2 — no false
positive); a real planted continuation lights up at *t* = +9.77 with a 78% win-rate. The detector
is live.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The box breakout does **not** beat a drift-matched random baseline
  (breakout − random = −16.4 / −14.8 / −8.2 / −9.2 bps at 5/10/20/60 days; the breakout-vs-random
  Welch *t* is **never positive** and never clears 2, most negative −1.56 at 5 days, *p* = 0.119).
  The impressive one-sample *t*'s (20-day +6.41, 60-day +6.67) are pure beta — the upward drift of
  long equity indices.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no residual edge once the drift you were always getting is
  removed, and costs only deepen the hole. The same drift is captured more cheaply and more fully
  by holding the index; the breakout rule trades less and pays costs on each breakout, dominating
  nothing. No capacity question because there is no edge to scale.
- **"Does the box breakout forecast"? — BUSTED.** The shuffled-box placebo leaves the result
  intact (*p* = 0.192): randomly-scattered entries do as well as the real breakouts, so the
  specific box-top timing carries no forecasting information. Darvas' box is a descriptive
  trade-management frame, not a forecasting edge on a diversified index tape.
